author: Linda Cook
title: Central DeWitt board OKs $33.7 million General Obligation Bond for Nov. 3 ballot - NewsBreak
text:
By Linda Cook ,
5 hours ago
The Central DeWitt Community School District Board of Education has accepted 346 certified petition signatures from community members, exceeding the requirement under Iowa law, and unanimously approved a resolution officially placing the district's proposed $33.7 million General Obligation Bond referendum on the Nov. 3 ballot.
With the petition requirement satisfied and the resolution approved, the district will continue
sharing information with the community ahead of the election, including project details,
conceptual renderings, community events, and facility tours. A community forum will begin at 6 p.m. Wednesday, Sept. 9, in the Central DeWitt Board Room.
For more information, including the full Facilities Master Plan, project renderings, upcoming
events, and frequently asked questions, is available on the district's 2026 Bond Referendum
website here .
“This proposed improvement plan addresses the district’s most pressing facility needs through
one coordinated effort rather than a series of disconnected repairs. It resolves nearly every
outstanding maintenance issue while modernizing our facilities, improving efficiency, and
creating better learning environments for students. Acting now also helps us stay ahead of rising
construction costs and reduce long-term maintenance expenses,” said Blake Thompson,
director of operations.
Board President Jodi Prosise said the board's action reflects extensive community input and
a continued commitment to transparency. "Reaching this milestone reflects the trust and
engagement of so many people across our community," said Prosise. "From the beginning,
our goal has been to make sure residents have clear, accurate information about these
proposed projects. We're grateful to everyone who signed the petition and to the volunteers
who made this possible, and we look forward to continuing that same open conversation with
voters between now and November."
The bond is part of the district's broader $54 million Facilities Master Plan, developed over several months with input from staff, parents, community members, and board representatives.
The plan centers on a PK–12 single campus model that brings all students together at the main
campus, with new high school academic spaces and new PK–2 learning environments created
within the existing facility.
The General Obligation Bond would provide 62% of total project funding, with the remaining
38% funded through state SAVE (one percent state sales tax) and PPEL (Physical Plant and
Equipment Levy) revenues. This approach allows the district to maximize existing resources
while limiting the amount that must be borrowed through the General Obligation Bond. By
combining these funding sources, the district can move the project forward without raising the
property tax rate.
Because the district paid off its previous bond ahead of schedule, the new bond would replace retiring debt at the same levy rate—extending the current rate rather than increasing it. Proposed improvements include: Full renovation of the current Intermediate School, including classrooms, finishes, HVAC, and roofing, to convert the building for PK-2 elementary use Renovations to the Middle School, including gym floor, HVAC, roofing, wrestling, fitness, and locker rooms Full renovation of the older portion of the existing high school, including classrooms, finishes, HVAC, and roofing A new high school addition featuring secure entry, academic classrooms, commons/cafeteria, and administrative offices Additional student parking, updated pick-up/drop-off loops, and site improvements to improve traffic flow across campus. "This plan is about more than buildings—it’s an investment in our community,” said Stephanie Mishler, Central DeWitt superintendent. “A single campus creates stronger connections, greater efficiencies, and more opportunities for students. Many critical parts of our facilities are already beyond their useful life, and when buildings and systems no longer work as they should, it affects the environment we create for students every day. This plan allows us to address those needs while creating better opportunities for the future. Now the choice belongs to our voters, and we encourage every community member to get informed, ask questions, and take part in that decision on Nov. 3.”
